newsitem.title: UK: Industry outlook brightens for world airshow.
newsitem.headline: Industry outlook brightens for world airshow.

text.p: Aircraft makers and their clients will be celebrating good times ahead at the Farnborough airshow next week as aircraft sales climb on a boom in air travel and as new models take to the skies.

The organisers, the Society of British Aerospace Companies (SBAC), said this year's show is 10 percent bigger than the last event in 1994. It expects some 250,000 people to visit over the week to view 1,165 exhibits and nearly 200 aircraft.
After eight years of Russian fighters stealing the show the European defence industry gets the chance of top billing for the flying display, with the debut of the Eurofighter jet.

The long-delayed 12 billion pounds ($18.71 billion) air superiority fighter, product of a consortium from Britain, Germany, Spain and Italy, will be out to impress its sponsor governments who are due to decide whether to put it into production this year.
But the sophisticated computer-controlled aircraft, which flew at Berlin this year and at Fairford in England last year, is still in development, so any aerobatics are going to be limited.
"The aircraft will not do a full display but it certainly will be a much more sporting display than it gave at Berlin," said a spokesman for partner British Aerospace.
However, Russia remains a strong force at air displays and is sending a new crowd-puller this year with the Farnborough debut for its super-agile Sukhoi Su-37 vectored fighter.
Meanwhile, the SBAC says it has been promised that the sinister U.S. bat-winged B-2A stealth bomber from Northrop Grumman will fly in on Monday.

But while the world's most advanced warplanes thunder around the southern English countryside the main dogfight on the ground will be between passenger jet giants Boeing Co and Airbus Industrie as they fight over new orders and try to sell rival plans for new large aircraft.
The record for new orders was at Farnborough 1990, the peak of the last boom in civil sales before recession took its toll. Orders were placed for 130 aircraft worth $14 billion.
Analysts say the current upturn is two or three years away from the same point in the cycle but should show a rise on Farnborough 1994, when there were nearly $3.0 billion of orders.
Analysts say that now airlines are making money again they are starting to order new aircraft to replace ageing fleets and to cope with extra traffic.

According to its own figures, the international airline industry made a collective net profit of $5.2 billion last year, up from $1.6 billion in 1994 and a loss of $4.1 billion in 1993, as growth in traffic led to full loads.

"In the past few years carriers have principally stuck with old equipment because it was cheap," said Chris Partridge of aircraft market consultants Avmark. "Now that they are actually making money I am sure that we will see some more orders, if only because the industry is growing so strongly at the moment."
"They can't turn up on Monday and not have something to crow about," said BZW analyst Nick Cunningham.
Orders this year show Boeing well in front but the European upstart has vowed to raise market share from 30-40 percent now to a regular 50 percent by the turn of the century.
A spokesman for Boeing said it has already sold 333 passenger aircraft worth $25.5 billion in the first eight months, after 346 aircraft worth $31 billion in all of 1995.
In the same period Airbus has booked in orders for 213 aircraft worth around $15 billion so far this year, against 106 aircraft worth $7.0 billion in all of 1995.
Industry sources said both companies are now working hard behind the scenes to drum up more order news for Farnborough.

Airbus is expected to have a follow-on order from Cathay Pacific for more A340 and A330s widebody jets, "but there are a number of other things which they hope will come through by the time they get to Farnborough," said one source.

Boeing is expected to confirm some options from British Airways on 747-400s but the sources said the order was likely to be for only a few aircraft and not the 30 which one newspaper predicted last week.
BA has already said it gradually plans to replace its older 747s with the latest version and it has "future delivery" options on 29 of the aircraft plus a further nine options.

However, the show's star turn may yet prove to be Boeing. The sources said it is still hoping to get advance orders from interested airlines in time to announce the launch of a superjumbo version of its 747 jet before Farnborough is over.
Analysts have variously estimated development costs for the new aircraft at anywhere between between $1.0 and $8.0 billion.

But the sources said Boeing is now racing to get the project launched before Airbus can tempt customers away with its proposals for a completely new aircraft of similar size - the Airbus A3XX, which could cost up to $15 billion.
